title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
summary: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.
text:
'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
- Published
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.
"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.
Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.
Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.
On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.
The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.
Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.
- Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather 
  - Published1 day ago
Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.
"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.
"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"
The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.
There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.
Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.
"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.
He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".
"We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving."
Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.

title: Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels
summary: A powerful storm knocked out power for nearly 1 million customers and flooded streets. And, experts predict inflation will not dampen American spending for the holidays
text:
Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels
Thanksgiving Storm Aftermath, Black Friday Economy, Eisenkot's Coalition Talks
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after a powerful storm swept through much of the East Coast and Midwest on Thanksgiving. Hundreds of flights were canceled and thousands were delayed during one of the busiest travel times of the year.
- 🎧 Flooding caused most of the damage and disruptions, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Several bridges in New Jersey were shut down, and people were seen kayaking through usually busy streets in parts of coastal Virginia. Exceptionally high tides, known as the King Tides, have been battering the West Coast. Lonsdorf says there's still a lot of work to do before roads return to normal, but there is some hope. The storms should move out and the tides should recede heading into Saturday, as people begin their journeys home.
Despite inflation and concerns about the cost of living, Americans are expected to spend a record amount again this year for Black Friday. The National Retail Federation predicts a 4.2% increase in holiday retail sales this year compared with last year.
- 🎧 NPR's Alina Selyukh says surveys indicate people are cutting back on other spending to spend during the holiday season. She notes that while gas and housing costs have been big drivers of inflation, the prices of goods, including gifts, have not risen as dramatically. She also says she's watching a shift in the trend of how people are shopping. Although most people are doing their holiday shopping online, more are choosing to shop in person.

Critics say the sweeping immigration changes have all but shut down access to asylum. Soon, the Supreme Court will consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections. In December, Justices will also review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to process asylum claims, even as some face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the asylum-seeker won't be returned to their home nation.

title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
text:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.
Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.
The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.
The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?
Surviving blackouts
Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.
Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.
I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

title: Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
summary: Pennsylvania and neighbouring states remain badly affected on Friday after both coasts were lashed with wind and rain.
text:
Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
- Published
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.
Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.
Conditions are now expected to improve, though forecasters caution that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms.
Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.
More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.
One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.
Parts of some states are under states of emergency, including New York.
Nearly 2in (5cm) of rain fell on New York City's iconic Central Park, making it the wettest Thanksgiving on record at that site as well, according to preliminary data, external from the NWS.
Organisers of the city's annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have also pushed back the event to Saturday - marking the event's first postponement in its 100-year history.
In neighbouring New Jersey, there were multiple reports of closed roads and bridges, and images of floodwater blanketing city streets.
"This is wild," an Ocean City, New Jersey-based blogger said in a video, external posted on social media, as he waded through water splashing above his waist.
- Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather 
  - Published1 day ago
The number of homes reporting power cuts peaked at close to a million on Thursday evening - with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey badly affected.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. In Maryland, almost two million customers were asked by authorities to limit their water consumption to essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
The storm is expected to ease on Friday and move into the Canadian provinces of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland on Saturday, leaving a much drier weekend for the north-eastern United States, according to the Met Office.

title: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
summary: The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
text:
French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.
Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.
Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.
The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning
With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.
He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.
On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.
"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.
Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").
The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.
"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.
Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate
The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
summary: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
text:
Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
- Published
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.
Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".
The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.
On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

  - Published7 days ago
- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend 
  - Published6 days ago
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.

title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
summary: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
text:
Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
- Published
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."
The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.
On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.
The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.
Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

  - Published55 minutes ago
Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.

title: From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
summary: A storm battered much of the country on Thursday, knocking out power to thousands of homes and disrupting travel. Today, Black Friday shopping deals kick off, and on Saturday New York City will hold the postponed Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
text:
From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
From blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
A massive storm that stretched from the Midwest to Manhattan left almost a million people without power by Thanksgiving evening and disrupted holiday travel.
More than 400 flights were cancelled and more than two thousand were delayed around the country on Thursday during one of the busiest travel times of the year. Driving was also made difficult by either heavy rains or snow and ice. Some 81.5 million people were expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.
Power was partially restored early Friday, but at the peak of the outage more than 980,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and elsewhere were without electricity. Missouri also suffered blackouts after heavy snowfall.
Several areas were also hit by major flooding, including Old Town Alexandria, Virginia, and Atlantic City, New Jersey, where some low-lying areas had close to 2 to 3 feet of water, according to city authorities.
And there's more flooding forecast. The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Washington DC area on Friday, saying the warning was in effect until 6 pm ET.
"The unprotected area on the Southwest Waterfront at the DC Seafood Market is expected to flood," the weather service said.
"Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. If travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth," the statement added.
On the other side of the country, the West Coast was hit by King Tides with strong waves battering the Bay Area in recent days. King Tides happen regularly, but they have been made worse by climate change and warming oceans, as well as a particularly strong El Niño.
Part of the Pacifica Pier south of San Francisco collapsed on Wednesday, roads saw some flooding and some homes along the coast have been affected.
New York City's Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record with 1.82 inches of rain. The city can expect strong winds on Friday, the weather service said, with gusts of up to 30 miles an hour.
Iconic Macy's parade postponed
Macy's annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in the city has been postponed for the first time in its history and will now take place on Saturday. While it's never been postponed before, it was cancelled altogether for several years during World War II.
Postponing it is causing major logistical problems, as there are around 11,000 participants in the parade, mostly volunteers, many of whom traveled in from out of state. But it's not safe to put up the iconic giant balloons the parade is known for during strong winds.

title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
summary: Paul Mackenzie is found guilty of killing his followers, weeks after being jailed for the mass murder of children.
text:
Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
- Published
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.
The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
Earlier this week, Mackenzie was also convicted of:
- assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child
- engaging in organised criminal activity
- radicalisation
- facilitating the commission of a terrorist act
- being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.

  - Published19 October
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.
A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".

Watch: Man and dog narrowly escape powerful king tide in Oregon

title: Can luxury save Macy's?
summary: This week's celebration of Macy's 100th Thanksgiving parade finds the department store at a turning point. After years of losing sales, the retailer is reimagining itself — as a higher-end destination.
text:
Can luxury save Macy's?
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.
"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."
As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.
The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.
How Macy's got squeezed in the middle
Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.
The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.
And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.
"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."
When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.
The way out is up
At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.
But it didn't work.
Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.
Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.
As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.
"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.
"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."
The new luxury vision
Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.
The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.

summary: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
text:
Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
- Published
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."
The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.
On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.
The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.
Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.
The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.

title: 'Think twice': Banff officials issue warning over thin ice after skater's death
summary: After three separate incidents, one fatal, at Lake Louise, Parks Canada is warning visitors to be cautious after a warmer than average November.
text:
'Think twice': Banff officials issue warning over thin ice after skater's death
- Published
A 70-year-old resident of Banff, Alberta, has died after falling through ice on Lake Louise, prompting warnings about outdoor safety as Canada experiences warmer than normal November temperatures.
Police said the man, who has not been identified, was ice skating alone on Tuesday evening when he fell through thin ice. He was found two hours later by a rescue team and pronounced dead at a nearby hospital.
It comes after two other ice skaters fell in the lake's frigid waters on Monday, though both survived.
Canadian park authorities have issued a warning to visitors of the world-famous Banff National Park urging them to "think twice" before stepping on the ice.
"Visitors must be able to self-rescue should they fall in the water," Parks Canada said in a notice posted on Monday.
"If you choose to skate on natural ice, you do so at your own risk."
In a statement, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police offered condolences to the 70-year-old's family. It also warned the public of the dangers of being on the ice.
Parks Canada said that early season ice can be unpredictable, and that it does not actively monitor natural ice surfaces for safety or mark potential hazards.
The incident comes as temperatures in Alberta and other parts of Canada have been warmer than average for this time of year.
Canada's largest city, Toronto, experienced unseasonable highs of 15C (59F) this month.
In Alberta, temperatures have been about three degrees Celsius warmer than what has been historically observed for November, Alysa Pederson, a meteorologist with Environment Canada, told the BBC.
On average, temperatures would dip below -10C for a number of days in November. But this year, Pederson noted that the coldest November day was -6C.
"It's going to become a challenge to form ice when your temperatures aren't really getting that cold," Pederson said.
Environment Canada's seasonal forecast suggests that much of Canada, external, from Vancouver to Halifax, will likely be seeing a warmer than average winter.
It is due partly to the weather phenomenon known as El Niño, where changing wind patterns over the Pacific Ocean result in heat being released into the atmosphere that can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.
"We're currently in a very strong El Niño event, potentially record-breaking by the time it peaks here in the next couple of months," Pederson explained.
She advised those who are eager to get outside in the winter to stay vigilant, as warmer weather can not only mean thin ice, but a higher risk of avalanches.
She added that while falling through ice in Banff is always a risk, the recent back-to-back incidents came as a surprise and called it "unfortunate".

title: Screen-free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
summary: Some parents, fed up with screens, have found an analog oasis in the role-playing game invented in the 1970s.
text:
Screen-free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
Dungeons & Dragons has captivated players for more than 50 years.
In its early days, some parents complained that the role-playing game kept kids holed up inside for hours at a time. NPR even did a 10-minute piece on it in 1979.
More recently, D&D has come back into popular culture through shows including Stranger Things, a 2023 blockbuster movie and an influx of interest during the COVID-19 lockdowns.
Now, what was once a nerdy pastime has become a screen-free parent's dream — a game that relies on imagination, a role of the dice and in-person communication.
"It's a great concoction," Ted Fair says. He's the (grown-up) Dungeon Master for a group of 9- to 12-year-old kids in Washington Heights in New York. "When you're able to sit down with … other people and harmonize like that."
Fair's group is part of Tweens Without Screens, a parent collective that focuses on providing technology-free activities for kids. They host events like knitting clubs and urban hikes. They have multiple D&D groups that meet monthly.
"I feel like part of what's kind of fun about it is we're trying to figure it out as we go along," said Rose Watson, a 12-year-old member of Fair's D&D crew.
In their most recent session, the group explored a cave and discovered a mysterious egg. Possibly a dragon egg? They didn't get a chance to find out! A low roll of the dice meant that instead of successfully stealing the egg, it crashed into pieces on the floor.
"It's like painting a picture in your mind," said Watson. She likes the in-person nature of the game. "A big part of it is getting together with other people and friendship and making jokes."
"And collaboration!" added her 9-year-old brother Leo Watson.
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
For fellow 9-year-old Amos Slodounik, it's about getting to try on a different personality.
"You can express yourself in different ways. You can be goofy and nobody will care," he said.
And for Benjamin Cho, also 9, the fun is in the imagination. He spent much of the session drawing elaborate tools and creatures for their game (a healing spider donut, for example). "I like D&D because there's a lot of items and things that you can make up."

title: Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
summary: France's president made the comment while speaking to French farming representatives, months after the EU banned Brazil beef and poultry products.
text:
Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
- Published
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron who called Brazilian meat "doped".
France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry which took effect in September.
In its statement, the Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".
Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.
In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.
Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.
"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.
Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".
Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".
Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

title: Analysis: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
summary: Other countries have rerouted trade in response to his first tariff salvo, now they are looking beyond Trump's tenure.
text:
Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
- Published
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.
Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.
"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.
Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.
The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.
Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.
The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.
It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.
The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".
The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

title: Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
summary: Trump's sweeping immigration changes — an asylum ban, mass firings and new legal maneuvers — have all but ended asylum. The high court will soon consider whether some shifts deny people due process.
text:
Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Critics say that combined, these moves have effectively shut down a once vital pathway for those fleeing persecution or danger.
The U.S. Supreme Court will soon consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections.
The legal challenge to the president's ban, which went into effect within hours of President Trump retaking office, is the latest legal case against the administration's seismic immigration policy changes that will be taken up by the high court. Those policy changes, critics say, have robbed asylum seekers of basic due process rights and have transformed the immigration court system into a deportation arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
In legal filings, the Trump administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and what the president and conservative critics have long said is abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Since it has been in place, the chaotic crush of people crossing into the U.S. has plummeted. U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions dropped to their lowest level in agency history this year. The agency recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.
"The difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow with the Border Security and Immigration Center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with Trump, told NPR. And should the Supreme Court reverse the ban, "it would be disastrous," he added.
Hankinson contends that most people arriving at the southern border don't qualify for asylum. "And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum, especially if they're coming from Venezuela or Afghanistan. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job," he said.
But, critics say, taken together the administration's moves have gutted access to asylum.
Despite newly restored quiet along the southern border, the president's argument for the asylum ban has been rejected by two lower federal courts. It has, however, remained largely in place as the case is tied up in court battles.

title: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
summary: The endangered reptiles were bound with duct tape to prevent them moving, officials say.
text:
Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
- Published
Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.
The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.
The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.
It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.
The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.
Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.
In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.
They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.
Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.
In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles, external that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.
Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases, external. Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

title: 12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start
summary: Here's something you can do as you gather with family and friends this holiday season: Take a free, five-minute quiz to assess your brain health. You'll learn simple changes to keep your mind sharp.
text:
12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start
Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.
It's one of the biggest fears about getting older: losing your memory. A growing body of evidence shows we can do a lot to lower the risk of dementia, starting with changes to our day-to-day habits.
For decades, dementia was seen as something determined by genes or bad luck: a disease that strikes late in life with little anyone can do about it. That thinking has radically changed.
In 2024, the Lancet Commission, an international panel of experts, identified 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia and estimated that about 45% of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed. And lifestyle changes, when sustained over time, can be a powerful form of prevention. Last year, a large clinical trial from the Alzheimer's Association, called U.S. POINTER, found that older adults at risk of cognitive decline who combined physical activity, healthy eating, cognitive exercises and social activity could protect brain health, thinking and memory.
A score for your brain
So where do you start? One good place is a free, five-minute online tool called the Brain Care Score. You can take it with friends and family members as you gather for the holidays.
It was developed by Jonathan Rosand, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, and his colleagues. It's now supported through the Global Brain Care Coalition.
"The Brain Care Score tells you how to reduce your risk of brain diseases in the future, especially dementia, stroke and depression," Rosand says. "And it tells you what you can do to live a longer, more flourishing life."
The score covers 12 factors in three areas. The higher your score, the lower your risk. Those factors are:
- Physical health: blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and body weight
- Lifestyle: diet, exercise, sleep, smoking and alcohol
- Social and emotional health: stress management, relationships and a sense of purpose
According to the coalition, the tool, "wasn't built to label risk. It was built to give people options and to show them that small changes made today can matter years from now."
Why blood pressure matters for your brain
High blood pressure might seem like a heart issue, but it's one of the biggest risk factors for dementia, and many people don't know their numbers.
"The higher your blood pressure, the more stress on your blood vessels," Rosand explains. "The more stress on your blood vessels, the more they break down over time," and the more they break down, the more likely they are to block or rupture. He says high blood pressure can increase the risk of stroke and dementia.
That's why the first step in calculating your score is to know your numbers: blood pressure, blood sugar (measured as A1c), cholesterol and body weight. You can ask your healthcare provider, check your patient portal or use a blood pressure cuff at a pharmacy. I

title: Ex-media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
summary: The former Murdoch media executive was overheard at an event referring to the way Grace Tame was dressed.
text:
Ex-media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
- Published
An Australian former media executive has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.
Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.
"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"
From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
